```latex
\paragraph{Cross-Architecture Verification (CAV).}
Let $M_1$ (generator) and $M_2$ (verifier) be models with 
architecturally independent inductive biases, i.e., their 
error sets satisfy $\text{Corr}(e_{M_1}, e_{M_2}) \approx 0$. 
Define the CAV ensemble prediction as:
\begin{equation}
  a^*_{\text{CAV}} = \arg\max_a \; 
    \text{votes}_{M_1}(a) + w \cdot \mathbb{1}[v_{M_2} = a],
\end{equation}
where $v_{M_2}$ is $M_2$'s independent verdict and $w$ 
controls the verifier's influence. Unlike same-model 
symbolic aggregation, where $\text{BR}(M_1, M_1) > 1$ 
causes systematic bias amplification (Proposition~1), 
the cross-architecture condition ensures 
$\text{BR}(M_1, M_2) \to 1$: the verifier's errors are 
uncorrelated with the generator's, providing genuine 
corrective signal on the generator's error subset. 
Formally, CAV improves over SC when:
\begin{equation}
  P(v_{M_2} = a^* \mid a_{M_1} \neq a^*) > 
  P(v_{M_2} \neq a^* \mid a_{M_1} = a^*),
\end{equation}
i.e., the verifier corrects the generator more often 
than it corrupts it --- a condition satisfied when 
$M_2$'s per-label accuracy exceeds chance on $M_1$'s 
error distribution.
```

```latex
\paragraph{Cross-Architecture Verification (CAV).}
Let $M_1$ (generator) and $M_2$ (verifier) be models with 
architecturally independent inductive biases, i.e., their 
error sets satisfy $\text{Corr}(e_{M_1}, e_{M_2}) \approx 0$.

\begin{equation}

    \text{votes}_{M_1}(a) + w \cdot \mathbb{1}[v_{M_2} = a],
\end{equation}

symbolic aggregation, where $\text{BR}(M_1, M_1) > 1$ 
causes systematic bias amplification (Proposition~1), 
the cross-architecture condition ensures 
$\text{BR}(M_1, M_2) \to 1$: the verifier's errors are 
uncorrelated with the generator's, providing genuine 
corrective signal on the generator's error subset. 
Formally, CAV improves over SC when:
\begin{equation}

  P(v_{M_2} \neq a^* \mid a_{M_1} = a^*),
\end{equation}

than it corrupts it --- a condition satisfied when 
$M_2$'s per-label accuracy exceeds chance on $M_1$'s 
error distribution.
```

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We identify the Symbolic Mirage: self-extracted symbolic constraints project the generating model's biases rather than providing independent verification, explaining why twenty-plus remediation strategies cannot break the same-model ceiling. Oracle controls confirm the mechanism is sound given uncontaminated constraints; a cross-architecture proof-of-concept escapes the mirage entirely. For practitioners, architecturally independent signals remain necessary for reliable constraint-based reasoning. Detecting the Symbolic Mirage in other self-verification domains is a critical open direction.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time computation scaling through multiple reasoning samples has emerged as a practical alternative to scaling model parameters \citep{snell2025scaling, guo2025deepseekr1}.
The dominant aggregation strategy, Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, samples $K$ chain-of-thought traces and selects the majority answer.
SC is simple, model-agnostic, and effective---but it is hitting a ceiling.
\citet{loo2025reevaluating} demonstrate that gains from increasing $K$ plateau and even decline for strong models.
The gap between SC's theoretical promise (independent correct voters converge to truth) and its practical behavior (saturating gains) points to a structural mismatch: same-model traces carry correlated errors, and majority voting has no mechanism to correct shared bias.

Confidence-weighted \citep{taubenfeld2025cisc} and universal \citep{chen2024usc} extensions alleviate this, but the core limitation persists.
Recent neuro-symbolic methods \citep{pan2023logiclm, olausson2023linc, xu2026dylos, li2025aristotle, wang2025fover, luo2025logicagent} report gains on logical reasoning but introduce components beyond the reasoning model.
A simpler question precedes these: can the \emph{same} model extract useful formal constraints from its own traces---a zero-cost upgrade requiring no additional model or data?
No prior work has systematically evaluated this.

We ground our analysis in the Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785}: if $K$ independent voters each answer correctly with probability $p > 0.5$, the majority converges to truth \citep{austensmith1996}.
When independence fails \citep{ladha1992correlated}, additional samples carry diminishing information.
Measuring inter-trace agreement with Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa}, we find $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across instruction-tuned conditions, yielding Effective-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ for nominal $K = 12$: traces beyond a dozen add negligible independent information (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
The bottleneck runs deeper than answer-level agreement suggests.
Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), revealing that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on final answers (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
When the same model extracts FOL constraints from these correlated traces, the constraints exhibit \emph{symbolic confirmation bias}: on problems where the model errs, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).
Self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires.

We study this through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
We evaluate SICA across six models (7B--32B), three reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}), and over 3,000 condition-evaluations (${\sim}$1,250 unique instances) with four-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
Twenty-plus remediation strategies spanning fifteen families---from prompt engineering through method-level redesign---all produce neutral or negative results, confirming the bottleneck is persistent at the 7B--32B scale.
While prior work qualitatively concludes that LLMs cannot self-correct or self-verify without external feedback \citep{huang2024selfcorrect, stechly2025selfverification}, we contribute reusable quantitative diagnostics (Effective-$K$, bias ratio), show that formal Z3-checked verification also fails, and reveal process-level reasoning homogeneity invisible to answer-only metrics.

Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound: same-model gold FOL yields $+29.90$\,pp (Mistral-7B) and $+14.22$\,pp (Qwen-14B) on FOLIO ($p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only ${\sim}$12\% of the same-model ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
The central finding is a persistent independence-accuracy trade-off: Debate reduces $\kappa$ from 0.44 to 0.15 (tripling Eff-$K$) but collapses accuracy by $-18.6$\,pp; SC, Diverse-Prompt, and ICG all cluster at $\kappa \approx 0.40$--$0.47$, forming a same-model ceiling that holds across three model families (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
A cross-architecture proof-of-concept suggests this gap is recoverable: DeBERTa-large NLI combined with SC yields $+3.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p = 0.013$, McNemar exact test) with consistent positive trends across datasets (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Independence-Accuracy Trade-off.} Same-model $\kappa \geq 0.40$ across four methods and three model families; twenty-plus remediation strategies (fifteen families) fail. A cross-architecture NLI verifier ($+3.50$\,pp on ProofWriter, $p = 0.013$) suggests the ceiling is escapable (\S\ref{sec:remediation}, \S\ref{sec:cross-arch}).

\item \textbf{Symbolic Confirmation Bias.} On incorrect problems, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).

\item \textbf{Process-Level Independence.} Across four model families, CoT cosine similarity ($0.69$--$0.79$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.45$--$0.74$); the gap intensifies with model capability, showing reasoning homogeneity is architecture-independent (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
\end{enumerate}
